reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Aubrey found a book at daycare. It had a dog on the front. The cover said DOG in big letters. Aubrey could see the word DOG matched the picture. "That word says dog," she said.

Miss Amy came over. "These books are from the library," she said. "We borrowed them. On Friday we take them all back."

Aubrey held the dog book tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

"No, sweetie," said Miss Amy. "Other kids want to read it too. That is why we bring it back."

Aubrey had a question. "Can I get it again after?"

"Yes," said Miss Amy. "You can borrow it lots of times."

Aubrey opened the book. She started at the front. She peeked at the dog on each page. She turned page after page until she got to the end.

A boy named Sam sat next to her. He looked sad. He did not have a book.

Aubrey handed him the dog book. "You can read it after me," she said. "Then we give it back on Friday. Then other kids read it too."

Sam smiled. He opened the front cover. He pointed at the word DOG. "This part says dog," he said.

"That's right," said Aubrey. Then she peeked over his shoulder at the pictures.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Ella wants to play house at daycare. But the baby doll has a scratch on its arm. "Oh no," says Ella. "The baby is hurt."

Ella holds the doll close. "Who will fix you?" she asks. Teacher Mia comes over. She is kind and warm. "You can fix the baby," she says.

Ella puts a soft bandage on the scratch. Then she wraps the doll in a small blanket. The doll stops looking hurt. Ella rocks it and sings, "Hush, little baby."

Tom wants to play too. He pretends to be the dog. He says, "Woof!" Ella laughs. Now they have a pretend house together.

"The baby feels better now," Ella says. "It feels better because I fixed the scratch." Teacher Mia smiles and sits right beside her. Ella gives the baby doll a big hug.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Nora looked out the big window. "Rain today!" she said. Raindrops went tap, tap, tap. Nora put on her rain boots. She held her umbrella up high.

Mama said, "Look at the sky now." The rain had stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny! "No rain boots in the sun," said Nora. She took them off. She put on her orange hat instead. "Sunny means hat!" said Nora.

Then the wind blew. Whoosh went the trees. Nora's hat flew off her head! She ran and ran. She caught her orange hat. Windy means hold on tight, she thought. She held it with both hands.

Nora sat down to paint a picture. She painted a turtle. She painted rain and sun and wind. "My turtle needs a hat too," said Nora. She painted a tiny orange hat on the turtle. "There!" said Nora. "Now my turtle is ready for sun, rain, and wind!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Isaiah sat on the rug in the living room. Uncle Ben held his phone up high. The big game was on the TV too. Isaiah had a loose tooth in his mouth. He wiggled it with his finger.

On the phone, the ball began to spin through the air. Then everyone shouted. Isaiah's mouth fell wide open. "It went in! We won!" He jumped up and down. His loose tooth did not fall out. It just wiggled some more.

But the TV still showed the ball in the air. Isaiah frowned. "Did I miss it?" he asked. He looked at the phone. Then he looked at the TV. The phone showed it first. The TV was slow. He waited and watched. The ball spun again on the big screen. Then the TV crowd shouted too. "It happens twice!" Isaiah said. He clapped with everyone. Dad lifted him up onto the couch, and Isaiah sat safe between Dad and Grandma.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Max went to Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big pink shell. "Put it to your ear," said Grandpa. Max listened. He heard a whoosh sound. "It sounds like the ocean!" said Max. His ears did that.

Grandpa said, "Let's play the sense game. I will hide something." Grandpa put a cookie in a box. Max could not see it. "My eyes miss it," said Max. He shook the box and heard a little rattle. His ears helped. He opened the box and smelled the cookie. His nose knew! Then he touched it. It was bumpy. His hands told him. Then he took a bite. Yum! His tongue did that.

"Five senses," said Max. "Ears, eyes, nose, hands, tongue."

"You are so brave to try with your eyes shut," said Grandpa. "Can ears really hear a snack?" Max laughed. "Yes! Ears hear the rattle!" Grandpa gave him one more cookie for winning the game.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ivy walked home with a small box. Inside was her first pet, a bunny named Pip. The snow fell on the street. Ivy held the box with both hands.

At home, Ivy put Pip on the floor. Pip sat very still. His nose did not move. Ivy wondered why. She looked at Pip. Then she looked at her own hand. It held a little carrot.

"Are you hungry?" she asked. Pip's nose began to wiggle. He hopped to the carrot. He ate it all up.

Ivy clapped. "The carrot made you hop!" she said. Now she knew. A bunny eats, then a bunny plays. So every morning, Ivy gave Pip his food first. Then Pip would hop and jump all day.

One day, Pip would not eat his carrot. Ivy looked in his bowl. The water was empty. She filled it up. Pip drank and drank. Then he ate his carrot. "Water first, food next," said Ivy. She patted his soft ears with her little hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Arya went to the library for song time. She wanted to sing her counting song. But the numbers fell out of her head!

She tried. "One, two, um, seven?"

The boy next to her laughed. "Seven comes after six, silly!"

Arya looked at the bookshelf. The librarian let her touch the spines. One book, two books, three books. She patted them like drums. Four, five, six. Then seven came right after six! Eight, nine, ten sat at the top of the shelf.

"Now I know," Arya said. "The numbers go in a line. They wait for turns!"

After songs, Dad gave her a salty cracker. Arya counted her bites. "One, two, three!" Then it was all gone.

"Ten more songs," said Arya, holding up just three fingers.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Rosalie stood by the big pool. The water smelled like sun and clean towels. Today was her first swim team meet. Her tummy felt flippy.

"Rosalie, you go second," said Coach Amy. "Wait for Ben to touch the wall. Then you jump in." Rosalie watched the light sparkle on the water. The whistle blew. Ben swam fast. His arms splashed. Rosalie got so excited. She jumped in too soon!

The coach held up a flat red sign. "Oh no," Rosalie said. "We have to start over. Why?" She watched the other team swim. Then she saw it. Ben had not touched the wall yet. The wall was like a tag in tag. You have to tag the wall first, then your friend can go. "I went before the tag," Rosalie said softly.

The team tried again. This time Rosalie waited. Ben slapped the wall. His hand made a clapping sound. Then Rosalie jumped. She kicked and kicked. Her team clapped for her at the end. "We did it!" Rosalie laughed. "The wall is the tag!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Ali stood in the backyard with Dad. Mom was inside with the new baby. Ali held his toy truck. He felt worried. "Will the baby take my toys?" he asked. Dad smiled. "Babies are too little for trucks," he said. "The baby cannot play yet. But you can hold her hand."

They went inside. Mom put the baby in Ali's arms. Ali sat very still. The baby was small and warm. Ali put his finger near her hand. The baby grabbed it. She held on tight! "She likes me," Ali said. "She is holding my finger."

Then the baby made a little sound. Her eyes closed. "She went to sleep," said Mom. "Babies sleep a lot." Ali sat and did not move his hand. He did not want to lose her grip. Dad sat close by. The baby held on, and Ali held on too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Anthony sat in the car with Dad. "We will meet Maria," said Dad. "She cuts hair in her salon." The salon was a little shop with a big window. Maria had a chair just for kids. It looked like a small red car with a steering wheel. Anthony sat in the car chair and held the wheel.

Maria snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some bits went down Anthony's collar. They stuck to his neck. They tickled and made him squirm. Maria laughed a kind laugh. She used a soft, poofy brush. She brushed his neck, and all the itchy bits fell away. Anthony patted his neck. "The hair bits made me itchy," he said. "The brush made the itchy stop."

Then Maria held up a mirror. Anthony saw a boy with short, neat hair. Was that really him? "That boy looks pretty sharp," said Dad. Anthony grinned at the mirror boy. The mirror boy grinned right back. Then Anthony turned the steering wheel and said, "Beep, beep! Let's go home!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Riley went to the vet with Dad. They picked up a small pet snake. His name was Pip.

At home, Riley gave Pip fresh water. The next day, the water looked cloudy. Pip hid in his little house. He would not come out. Riley put a pinky mouse in his home. Pip did not eat it. Riley waited. She waited all day. Still, Pip stayed inside.

Riley looked at the cloudy water. "The water is old," she said. She took the bowl out. She washed it with warm water. She filled it with clean water. She set it back in, nice and slow. Then she sorted the pinky mice and put one by the bowl. Pip came out. He drank and drank. Then he ate his mouse.

"The clean water helped," Riley said. She smiled at Pip. "I will change your water every day."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Elena went to the park with her mama. She wanted to draw with her new chalk on the sidewalk. The sun was hot on the ground. "The chalk is too hot," Elena said. She put it in the shade. She waited and waited.

Then Elena touched the chalk again. "Now it is cold," she said. The big tree made the shade. The shade made the chalk cold. Elena smiled. She began to draw a big cat. She drew a small cat too.

A dog ran by, very fast. A turtle walked by, very slow. Elena drew a fast dog. She drew a slow turtle. "What is your cat's name?" mama asked. "Cat," said Elena. She drew and drew until the sun went down. "Time to go, Elena," said mama. Elena picked up her cold chalk. "Bye bye, park," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Jasmine ran to the sandbox with her bunny. She wanted to play house. But bunny was cold. The wind blew hard.

Jasmine saw Ben by the slide. He had a friendly face. He was wrapping his truck in a scarf. "My truck is a baby," said Ben. "Babies need warm blankets." Jasmine looked at her bunny. Bunny was a baby too. Babies need warm things.

She found a leaf and a big red cup. She put the leaf in the cup. Then she put bunny on the leaf. She mixed sand and water in a pot. It became a smooth grey cake. "Time for dinner, baby bunny," she said. Bunny sat by the pretend stove.

Ben came over with his truck baby. The truck baby ate sand cake too. "Our babies are warm now," said Jasmine. "Because we wrapped them up." The wind kept blowing. But the babies slept snug in the cup and the scarf. Jasmine patted bunny on the head. "Goodnight, baby," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan wanted to wash his toy truck. The truck was covered in paint from art time. Red paint, blue paint, and sticky paint too. So Declan ran to the bathroom. He stood on his little stool by the sink.

First, he turned one tap. The water felt cold. Brrr, cold like ice. Then he turned the other tap. The water got warm, then hot. Declan pulled his hand back fast. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He turned the hot tap back, just a tiny bit. Now the water was warm and nice. Why did the water change? Because that tap was the hot one. He knew it now.

He soaped the truck and rubbed the paint off. Bubbles grew big and shiny. They smelled like lemons. Then he saw something. A small silver razor sat by the sink. Dad's razor. It looked shiny and new. Could he touch it? Declan looked at it. It was sharp, like a tiny knife. He kept his hands in the warm water instead.

"Mama, come see!" he called. He liked to stay close to Mama in the bathroom. Mama came and stood by the door. Then, surprise! The toy truck was not alone. A tiny shy frog sat on the soap dish. "Hello, frog," said Declan. "Do you like warm water too?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Emile sat on the cold floor at daycare. He found a box of wooden blocks. He wished to build a tall, tall tower. He put a circle block on the bottom. He put a square block on top.

The tower wobbled. Then it fell over. The circle block rolled away across the rug. "Oh no," said Emile. He picked up the circle block. It rolled again, right out of his hand.

Emile looked at the blocks. He put a square block on the bottom. Squares had flat sides. Flat sides did not roll. He put another square on top. Then a rectangle. Then a triangle, like a little roof.

"Look, Miss Ana!" said Emile. "My tower stands up!"

"It stands because the bottom does not roll," said Miss Ana.

Emile nodded. "Circles roll. Squars stay still." He placed his shoe next to the tower. "My shoe is flat too. It helps the tower stand." The tower stood tall and still, all through play time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Billie went to the playground after school. Her grandma came too. The sun was big and bright. Some slides sat in the sun. Some slides sat in the shade.

Billie wanted to go down the big slide. She put her hand on it first. The slide was very hot. She pulled her hand back fast. "The sun made it hot," she said. Then she saw the little slide under the tree. She touched it. That one was cool. "The tree made shade," she said. So she slid down the cool slide, again and again.

Near the fence, Billie saw a shiny can on the ground. She wanted to pick it up. Then she remembered. "I don't touch cans," she said. "They are not mine." She looked for grandma instead. Grandma sat on a lazy old bench under the tree. Billie held her hand the whole way home. "Stay close," said grandma. And Billie did.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Matteo sat in his car seat. "Let's count red cars!" said Dad. "We need ten." Matteo loved red cars. He wanted to find them all.

"One, two, three," said Matteo. A red car went by. "Five!" he shouted. Dad laughed. "Five is old news. One comes after three. Try again, big guy." Matteo frowned. Then he sang his counting song in his head, the one his teacher sang at school. "One, two, three, four, five!" The words came out in the right order, like steps on stairs. Each word had its own place.

Another red car drove past. "Six!" yelled Matteo. Then seven, then eight, then nine. One more red car came around the bend. Matteo bounced in his seat. "Ten! Ten red cars!" He clapped his hands. "The song helped me! The numbers go in a line!" Dad beeped the horn twice. "You did it, Matteo. Now let's count blue trucks!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Eloise sat in the big red seat. Her favorite team was on the field. Dad was next to her. Grandma was next to Dad. Uncle Ben was next to Grandma. One, two, three, four people in a row.

Eloise wanted to tell Dad something. She saw a player drop the ball. She opened her mouth to speak. Then the crowd jumped up. Everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" The noise was like thunder. Dad could not hear her at all.

So Eloise waited. The players lined up. The crowd sat down. The stadium got quiet.

"Now," said Eloise. "The crowd sat down. That is why it is quiet now."

Dad laughed and clapped. "You cleaned your cup and your ears too," he said.

Eloise smiled. The loud game felt like a dream. "One, two, three," she said. "Watch with me."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Ruby sat at the little red table. On it lay a shiny string of beads. Her teacher, Miss Pam, had a question.

"Ruby, which string has more beads? This one, or that one?"

Ruby wanted to be right. She lifted the shiny string. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." The last bead was blue. "Five," she said. "Five beads."

Then Ruby had a worry. What if she counted the blue one first? Would it be different? She asked herself, "What will I get?"

She counted again. She started at the blue bead this time. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five.

"It is five both ways," Ruby said. She counted the other string. It had four beads. "This one has more. This one has five."

Miss Pam smiled. "Good counting, Ruby."

Ruby held up the shiny string. "Five," she said. "Five both ways."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Lea was going on a trip with her family. They packed a big bag. They drove a long, long way. Then they came to a beach. It was not like home. The sand was different. The water went on and on.

Lea had her rubber duck from her house in her hand. "Duck wants to swim," she said. She put the duck in the sea. The duck did not sink. It sat on top of the water. "Look, it floats!" said Lea.

Her brother Tom pushed the duck down. The duck popped back up. It went bloop! Lea laughed. "Silly duck," she said. She pushed it down too. Bloop! Up it came again. "It floats because it is full of air," said Lea. She squeezed the duck. It squeaked in her hand.

"Air inside, up it goes," said Tom. They played until the sun went low. Lea held her duck tight. "You can sleep in a different house tonight," she told it. The duck squeaked all the way up the beach.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Athena sat at the big piano. Her teacher, Miss Kim, stood beside her. Athena wanted to play the rain song. She hit the keys very fast. Boom, boom, boom! The sound was so big.

"Why is it so loud?" Athena asked.

Miss Kim did not say. She just smiled. Athena tried again. This time she pressed the keys slowly and gently. Tip, tip, tip. The sound was tiny, like soft rain.

"Slow fingers make soft sound," said Athena. She pressed slow again. Tip, tip, tip. It worked! She made a stormy part with fast, hard fingers. Boom! Then a quiet part with slow fingers. Tip, tip, tip.

Miss Kim showed Athena a picture of rain clouds. Athena played along with it. Fast for the storm. Slow for the little drops.

At the end, Athena gave Miss Kim a hug. "Thank you," she said. Then she played the rain song one more time, tip, tip, boom!

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Nolan went to the community garden with Grandma. He held a little bag of carrot seeds. The seeds were tiny and smooth. Nolan rubbed them between his fingers.

He dug a small hole. He put the seeds in. He patted the dirt down. Then he ran to the pond with his small red cup. He filled it up. He poured water on the dirt.

"Will the seeds grow today?" he asked. "No," said Grandma. "First they drink the water. Then little green tops pop up."

Every day Nolan filled his cup at the pond. Every day he watered his seeds. One morning he saw something green. "The water made them grow!" said Nolan. He jumped up and down. A tiny green top was peeking out of the dirt.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Theodore ran to the farmers' market with Mama. He held her hand the whole way. The market was big and loud and full of colors.

"I will cook for the family," said Theodore. "I will make butter!" He found a farmer with white cream in a jar. "Can I buy it? Please?" He paid with his own coins. He was so proud.

At home, Theodore poured the cream into a little jar. He put the lid on tight. He knocked on the lid two times, like a little drum. Then he shook the jar. He shook it fast. He shook it slow. He shook it and shook it.

At first the cream just sloshed. Theodore kept shaking. Then something changed. The sloshing stopped. Something hard was bumping inside the jar. He opened the lid and looked. A yellow lump sat in thin white milk. "Mama! Papa! Come see!" he called. "I shook the cream, and it turned into butter!" He shook it, and that made it happen.

Papa warmed a pan. Theodore spread his butter on hot toast. The butter melted right away, all shiny. He cut the toast into a lion shape. The lion had a buttery mane.

"Theodore made this!" said Papa, taking a big bite.

"More shaking tomorrow!" said Theodore, and he shook the empty jar one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Lucy woke up and saw white. Snow had come in the night. No school today. Mom said, "It is a snow day." Lucy put on her red boots. She tried to lock the door behind her, but her mittens were too big. Mom helped with the lock, and they laughed.

They went to the big hill. Lucy sat on her sled. Mom gave one little push. The sled went fast, so fast. Lucy rolled into the soft snow. A small brown leaf sat on top of the snow. Lucy picked it up. It looked funny with little white dots on it.

Lucy looked at the leaf. "The snow fell on you," she said. She looked at the hill. "The hill is fast because the snow is on it." She climbed up again, holding the leaf. "Ready, Mom!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Maverick sat at the little blue table. He was making a lion. He glued on the mane. He glued on the eyes. He glued on the long paper tail.

Then Maverick wanted more glue. He squeezed the bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. One dot, two dots, three dots, four dots. The glue made a big wet puddle.

"Uh oh," said Maverick. "Why is my lion bumpy?" He looked closely. He touched the paper. It was soft and soggy. "Too much glue," he said. "The wet glue made my paper wrinkle."

His friend Nia sat next to him. She held out her glue stick. "You can use mine," she said. "It makes small dots." Nia was kind to share.

Maverick took the glue stick. He made one small dot. Then one more. The new paper tail stayed flat. He stuck it on the lion.

"Thank you, Nia," said Maverick. He held up his lion. The long tail swung back and forth. "Roar!" said Maverick, and Nia laughed and roared too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Brielle stood in the sunny backyard. She had a red beanbag and a big blue ball. She wanted to toss the beanbag into the hoop.

"One, two, three, throw!" she said. The beanbag flew up. It came down in the grass. Not in the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle. She tried again. "One, two, three, throw!" This time she threw it softly. The beanbag went up. It went down. It landed right in the hoop. Brielle jumped. "Soft hands, soft throw!" she said. She clapped and clapped.

Then Papa rolled the big blue ball to her. Brielle held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. It rolled under the bush. "Come back, ball!" she said. Papa rolled it again. This time Brielle held out both hands. She opened them wide, like a big bowl. The ball came. The ball landed. She caught it with both hands!

"I caught it! I caught it!" said Brielle. The wind began to blow her hair. Papa laughed at the sound of her happy squeal. "Again!" said Brielle. "One, two, three, roll!" Papa bent down and rolled the ball back across the grass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Claire stood at the front door. She wanted to sail her little red boat in a puddle. But where was a puddle? Yesterday it was rainy. Big puddles had filled the street. Claire had worn her yellow raincoat and boots.

Today the sun was bright. Claire looked down. The puddles were gone. The raincoat was too hot, so she took it off. "The sun made the water melt away," she said. "That is why the puddle is gone."

Then the wind blew. It pushed her hair all around. It was windy too. Claire held her boat tight.

Her brother Sam came to the door. He had no hat. His ears looked cold. Claire ran and got his blue hat. "Here, Sam," she said. "The wind is strong."

Sam put on the hat. Then they saw white dots falling. Snow! It fell on the boat and did not melt.

Claire opened the door wide. "Snow boat race!" she shouted.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Layla ran to the toy corner. The big red truck was there. She wanted it so much.

But Ben had the truck first. He was pushing it up a hill of blocks. Layla reached out her hand to grab it. Then she stopped. She saw the teacher's sand timer on the shelf. The teacher had shown them how it works. You flip it over, and the sand falls down. When all the sand is gone, the turn is done.

Layla asked, "Can I have the next turn?" Ben said, "Okay." He flipped the timer. Layla sat down on the rug to wait. The sand fell slow, little by little. She counted the grains she could see.

At last the sand stopped. "Your turn now," said Ben. He handed her the truck. Layla pushed it fast across the rug. She grinned and said, "The sand said it is my turn!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Ibrahim went to the park with Mama. He had his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. At the slide, he put the car down. Then he ran to the swings. When he came back, the car was gone.

"Where is my car?" he asked. He looked by the slide. No car. He looked in the sandbox. No car. Mama said, "Try to remember. Where did you play last?" Ibrahim thought hard. "The slide," he said. "I put it down there."

The winter wind blew cold on his face. The leaves on the ground moved. They moved all together, in one way. Then Ibrahim saw it. The wind had pushed his car. It had rolled under the bench!

He got down on his knees. His hand touched something smooth and cold. It was the blue car. "The wind moved it!" he said. "The wind made it roll under here."

Mama smiled and helped him up. "Good looking, Ibrahim," she said. He held the car tight in his warm hand. "You stay with me now," he told it. The wind blew again. Ibrahim laughed, and put the car in his pocket, all safe.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Leah sat on the big soft rug in the living room. Daddy's tablet lay on the table. It was dark and still. Leah wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped again. Still nothing. Then she found the little button on the side. She held the button down with her finger. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen grew bright. "The button makes it wake up," said Leah. She asked herself, "Now what?" The little picture of a crayon sat in the corner. She touched it. The drawing app opened.

Leah drew a big orange cat. She held the tablet with both hands while she drew. After a while, the tablet felt a little hot near the bottom. "Time to stop," said Daddy with a smile. Leah pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She carried the tablet to the shelf and set it down, just like Daddy showed her.

"It sleeps now, like I sleep in my bed," said Leah. Daddy laughed softly. "Yes, it rests till tomorrow." Leah patted the dark screen. "Night night, tablet."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Theo put on his favorite shirt. It had a yellow duck on the front. He was going to the music room at the community center.

A big rainbow xylophone sat on the table. Theo wanted to play his song. He hit the bars fast, all over. The sounds went boom, boom, boom. It did not sound like a song. It sounded like big feet stomping.

Theo stopped and looked at the bars. He tapped a long bar. It made a low sound. He tapped a short bar. It made a high sound. He tapped the short bars, one, two, three. Ding, ding, ding. "The small ones go up high," Theo said.

He played the short bars again, slow this time. Ding, ding, ding. The lady next to him clapped her hands. Theo patted his duck shirt. Then he played his high song one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Isabelle went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. It was a rainy day, so her shoes were wet and muddy. Outside the big hall, everyone was taking off their shoes. Isabelle saw lots of shoes in little rows. She held Mama's hand tight. "Why do the shoes come off?" she asked. Mama said, "You will see."

Isabelle pulled off her boots. She put them in a row next to Papa's shoes. Then she walked inside. The floor was warm and soft on her feet. She looked back at the door. A man with muddy boots came in without taking them off. His boots made brown marks on the clean floor. A lady wiped the marks with a cloth.

"That is why," said Isabelle. "Shoes off, floor stays clean." Mama smiled and picked her up. There were candles and flowers everywhere. Grandma was there too. She had a cough, and Mama gave her some medicine with water. After, Grandma took Isabelle to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat," she said. Isabelle liked the warm water. It was like a little bath for her hands. Then they sat down together, and Isabelle ate a sweet, round piece of fruit. "Mmm," she said. "More, please."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
David put on his little apron. Today he would bake fox cookies for his family. The teacher, Miss Ana, stood close by his side.

"Let's read the recipe together," said Miss Ana. David read the picture list. Flour, butter, honey. He mixed everything in a big bowl. The dough felt soft and squishy. David pressed the fox cookie cutter down. Out came a fox shape, one, two, three.

He licked his finger. "The honey is so sweet," he said. Then he put the fox cookies on a tray. Miss Ana slid the tray into the warm oven. David waited and watched through the glass.

The soft dough changed. It got firm and a little brown. "The hot oven makes it hard," David said. Miss Ana smiled and nodded.

Soon the cookies came out. They were crisp foxes, ready for Mom and Dad. David put them in his little box. He held Miss Ana's hand all the way to the car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Florence went to the hospital with her dad. Her mum had a new baby. "A baby brother," said Dad. "His name is Sam."

Florence held up her picture. "I draw a dog for Sam," she said. But Sam did not look. Florence waved. Sam did not look. "Did I do it wrong?" she asked.

Dad said, "Try again. Come close." Florence leaned in near Sam's face. She held her soft toy mouse. Sam opened his eyes. Sam looked and looked. "Babies see things best close up," said Mum. "So that is why," said Florence. "Babies see close up."

Sam made a small sound. It was like a tiny cat. Florence sang softly. Sam moved his hand. Florence touched one little finger. "Hello, Sam," she said. "This is my mouse."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Ali ran into the big kitchen. Snow was falling outside the window. "Today I help!" he said.

Nana gave him warm toast. The butter was cold and hard. Ali pushed it. It would not spread. The toast tore. Then Nana set the toast near the warm stove. Ali tried again. The butter was soft now. It spread all over. "Soft butter goes on easy!" said Ali.

Next came the milk. Ali held the little cup with two hands. He tipped the jug fast. Milk splashed out. "Too fast," said Ali. He tipped it slow, just a little. The milk went in. Not one drop fell. "Slow pour, no spill!" said Ali. He looked at his cute cup, so full and white. Ali took a big drink. "More toast, please!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eva went to the library with her dad. She saw a book about a red dragon. Eva loved dragons. She grabbed it fast.

A girl sat at a little table. She was reading a book. She held it up. "See? You start here," the girl said. She pointed to the front. She turned the pages one by one. Eva looked at her own book. Little marks ran across every page. "The marks talk," the girl said. "Dad reads them to me." Eva pressed her ear to the page. The page was quiet. But when Dad read it, the dragon roared. The marks really did talk!

Eva held the dragon book tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Dad shook his head. "We take it home for a while. Then we bring it back. Other kids read it too." Eva frowned. Then she thought of the girl. The girl might want the dragon book next. "Okay," Eva said. "But I get the last hug." She hugged the dragon one time. Then she put it in Dad's bag. "Bye, dragon," she whispered. "Roar for the next kid."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Leah hurried to the play corner at school. Her baby doll was in the crib. Her friend Max said, "The baby is crying. She is hungry." Leah looked for a bottle. She could not find one. The bottle was lost.

Then Leah saw a small yellow bucket. It was hard and shiny. She tipped it upside down. It looked just like a bottle! Leah held it to the baby's mouth. "Drink your milk," she said softly. Max tapped the bucket with his hand. "More milk, baby," he said. The baby drank and drank. Soon Leah laid her down in the crib. She covered her with a small cloth blanket.

Max clapped his hands. "The baby stopped crying because you fed her," he said. Leah smiled and patted the doll's head. "Sleep now, baby," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Everly was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Everly wanted to hold the baby. But Mom said, "Not yet. The baby needs to eat first."

The baby was hungry. She cried and cried. Everly covered her ears. "Why is she so loud?" asked Everly. Grandma was cooking soup at the stove. "Babies cry when they need something," said Grandma. "This baby needs milk."

Mom sat in the big chair. She fed the baby milk. The baby drank. The crying stopped. Everly listened. The house was quiet now. "She cried because she was hungry," said Everly. "Now her tummy is full."

The soup was too hot. Grandma blew on it. "We will let it cool," she said. Everly waited at the table. Then Mom said, "Now you can sit by the baby." Everly sat very still. She touched the baby's tiny hand. The baby held on tight. Everly smiled and whispered, "Hello, baby sister."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Nova ran to the block corner at daycare. She was excited to build a tall tower.

Her friend Leo was there first. Nova grabbed a red block. Leo yelled and pushed the blocks down. Now Leo looked angry. His face was red and tight.

Nova felt scared. She ran to Teacher Mia. "Leo pushed the blocks," she said. "I am afraid of him."

Teacher Mia held her hand. "Stay here with me," she said. "Let us look at Leo."

Leo sat on the floor now. He cried big tears. His face was sad.

"His blocks fell down," said Nova. "That is why he is mad."

Teacher Mia nodded. Nova picked up one block. She gave it to Leo. Leo wiped his eyes and smiled.

"Want to build with me?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Nova. They stacked blocks high, high, high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Mason saw his toy lion up on the big shelf. He wanted it so much. He reached up. His hand was too small. The lion did not move.

Mason tried to shake the shelf a little. The lion still did not come down. He felt like crying. Then Dad walked in. "Dad, please help," Mason said. Dad smiled. "Of course! You asked so nicely." Dad lifted the lion down.

"Thank you, Dad," said Mason. He hugged his lion tight. Then he ran fast, and he bumped into Dad's leg. "Sorry, Dad," said Mason. Dad gave him a kiss on the head. "That's okay," said Dad.

Mason sat on the soft rug. He held his lion. "I said please," Mason said. "Then you helped me." Dad sat down too. "That's right," said Dad. Mason made the lion shake its mane. "Roar," said Mason softly. Dad laughed. Mason laughed too. The lion got a big goodnight hug.
